The analyzer minted `union` and published every read and call inside it under that source; the truth derived `@"union"` raw and did not recognise the scope. An `identifier` node's text carries the `@"..."` syntax and the published name does not, so the two keys could never meet. Z41 (a read name looked up raw) and Z43 (a verifier key built from raw text) were this same mistake; this was the FOURTH site, in the enclosing-scope extraction of `deriveZigEdgesWithSource` — and fixing the first site did not fix it, because there are two copies of the scope rule and I had patched one.
decisions.resolution: Every point in the truth where an identifier NODE becomes a NAME is now canonicalized: the enclosing scope on both edge passes, the container owner, the container name, the generic-function set, the type-name set, and the field/callee leaf. `uses`/`calls` at 3,839 files: **AGREE 290,530, PHANTOM 0, MISSING 0**.
decisions.cost: Four sites, four fixes, one rule that was never written as a rule. And a fifth lesson attached to the fix rather than the defect: the FIRST patch landed on the bare-read pass and the full-corpus re-run still reported 364 rows, because I had patched one copy of a two-copy rule. The second copy was found by re-running the same full-corpus gate, not by reading the first patch's neighbourhood — which is the argument for re-running the expensive instrument instead of trusting the cheap fix.

decisions.wave: 14 - one syntactic occurrence, two edges, two confidences
decisions.status: FIXED - the two `uses` passes deduped independently
decisions.observation: At full corpus, 16 rows in 7 files were DUPLICATE edges: the same type, source, target and line published twice with conflicting metadata — `uses main -> foo` as `zig_field_access` @ 0.75 and again as `identifier_usage` @ 1.0, from `zig/test/standalone/dep_mutually_recursive/test.zig:5`.
decisions.analysis: `analyzeZigCodeRelationships` dedupes field reads in `emittedUses` keyed `${source}->${field}`; `analyzeZigBareIdentifierUses` dedupes bare reads in its own `emitted` keyed `${src}::uses::${name}`. Different methods, different sets, different key formats — so a name derivable BOTH ways is published twice. It happens when a field-expression leaf happens to share a name with a file-scope value: `foo` in `x.foo` is a member access AND a resolvable name. A consumer cannot resolve that edge — two rows, one relationship, two confidences, no rule for which wins.
decisions.resolution: One dedupe after both passes: one `uses` edge per (source, target), keeping the HIGHER confidence, which is also the more accurate — `identifier_usage` @ 1.0 means the name RESOLVES to a file-scope value (a fact), while `zig_field_access` @ 0.75 is the inference that the leaf is a member. The winner keeps its reason code, so the edge still records which derivation it came from.

decisions.wave: 14 - the last two rows in 3,839 files
decisions.status: FIXED both - and one of them was the ORACLE's fault, not the analyzer's
decisions.observation: With everything else at 0, the full-corpus run left exactly two classes: `contains Prefix -> =` (a field named `=`, which Zig allows) and `references (global) -> ` (an EMPTY target, from `@import("")` in compile_errors/invalid_identifiers.zig). Plus `contains -> _` × 3, which the name-level gate had been reporting as unexplained.
decisions.analysis: The `_` rows are the interesting ones and the TRUTH was wrong: `const Label = enum { @"0:", @"1:", …, @"_", pseudo }` in zig's x86 backend is an EXPLICITLY QUOTED member name — a real, deliberately named enum member — and the truth tested the blank identifier on the CANONICALIZED name, so it discarded `@"_"` along with `const _ = 1;`. That is Z46's distinction (a blank in a BINDING is a discard; a blank in a DECLARATION is a name) applied to the oracle for the first time. The empty target is a genuine analyzer defect: an `@import` whose path is empty names no module, so both the record and its `references` twin are edges into nothing.
decisions.resolution: The truth's blank-identifier test now runs on the RAW spelling (`_` exactly is the blank identifier; `@"_"` is a name), at both import sites the analyzer suppresses an empty target rather than publishing an unresolvable edge, and the invariant's operator-name set learned `=`.
decisions.cost: The full-corpus run also proved my own invariant gate wrong in FOUR places — `contains` is symbol-keyed and legitimately repeats a (owner, member) 3,353 times; self-loops are legal for `uses` (a local named after its function, 372), `contains` (a container with a member of its own name, 12) and `instantiates` (a construction inside the type's own declaration, 142), not only for `calls`; and Zig permits operator-named fields. A gate calibrated on 200 files does not survive the tail, and neither did mine. It now encodes what the corpus says rather than what a sample suggested.

decisions.wave: 15 - the probe's own bucket, before any of its numbers were published
decisions.status: MEASUREMENT CORRECTED - the cross-file ceiling is trustworthy only after this
decisions.observation: `zigw-crossfile.ts` counted EVERY `struct_initializer` whose type leaf is not declared in this file as a candidate cross-file construction: 96,277 rows at full corpus. Its own sample was `[0][]const u8` — an ARRAY expression, not a construction. Publishing a ceiling derived from that bucket would have overstated the remaining work by roughly an order of magnitude.
decisions.analysis: A construction of a NAMED type has an `identifier` or a `field_expression` as its type child. `.{ .a = 1 }` (anonymous) and `[_]struct { A, B }{ ... }` (a type expression) are not constructions of a named type and cannot be cross-file instantiations. Split into three buckets instead of one: named-and-imported (578, genuine candidates), named-but-not-declared-here (1,860, mostly `[1]graphics.Glyph`-shaped TYPE expressions), and anonymous/type-expression (93,839).
decisions.cost: Fifth instrument of mine to be wrong about what it was counting, and the first one where publishing the number BEFORE fixing the instrument would have been the mistake — every earlier one this session was caught before it reached a document, and this one was caught by reading the sample attached to the number I was about to quote. An unexamined count is not a measurement, and a mis-categorised count is worse than no count, because it looks like scope.

decisions.wave: 16 - the quoting rule, SEVENTH and EIGHTH sites, and then an exhaustive sweep
decisions.status: FIXED - the sweep is now exhaustive, not reactive
decisions.observation: The master review re-ran the full-corpus `instantiates` gate and found 2 PHANTOM and 2 MISSING rows — four rows of noise from ONE missing canonicalizer, in two files a 200-file draw never reaches: `zig/lib/std/zig/llvm/Builder.zig:5361` and `zls/src/features/workspace_symbols.zig:51`.
decisions.analysis: Both were the `from` (enclosing scope), not the target. `Builder.zig` has a function literally named `@"switch"` (the LLVM switch-instruction emitter, quoted because `switch` is a keyword), and `deriveZigInstantiation` carries its OWN local `enclosing()` helper that Z51's fix never touched — it was a third copy of the scope rule alongside the two in the edge derivations. Fixing the first two had left this one, which is why the class reappeared at full corpus and not at 200.
decisions.resolution: Rather than patch site seven and hope, the sweep was made EXHAUSTIVE: every place in `script/m14/zig-truth.ts` where an identifier NODE becomes a NAME is now canonicalized, and the sweep was verified by asserting that ZERO raw `return String(<node>.text)` name reads remain in the file. That is the first pass in this lane's history that was exhaustive rather than reactive, and it is why this class did not come back a third time.
decisions.cost: Exhaustive sweeping is only safe when the ORDERING of two rules is respected, and getting that wrong caused the one regression of this wave — see Z56. Eight sites for one rule, over five waves, is the cost of never writing the rule down as a rule.

decisions.wave: 16 - the regression the exhaustive sweep caused, and why it is an ordering bug
decisions.status: FIXED - the two rules are ordered, not competing
decisions.observation: Making the sweep exhaustive immediately REBROKE Z53: the full-corpus gate went from `contains` 0 phantom / `unexplained` 0 to **PHANTOM 3 / 2 classes**, and the samples were the Z53 rows verbatim — `contains Label -> _` in zig's x86 backend.
decisions.analysis: Z53 tells a DISCARD (`const _ = 1;`, node text exactly `_`) from a REAL quoted member name (`@"_"`, an enum member deliberately spelled that way) by comparing the **RAW** spelling. The sweep canonicalized `firstIdent`, which is what feeds that test — so `@"_"` and `_` both arrived as `_`, the blank test fired, and the real member was dropped again. The two rules are not in conflict; they are ORDERED: read the node RAW, decide blank-or-name on the raw spelling, and canonicalize only when building the NAME. Canonicalizing one step earlier destroys the information the decision needs.
decisions.resolution: `firstIdent` returns the raw text again, and `push()` canonicalizes AFTER the blank-identifier test. Re-measured: `contains` 0 phantom / 0 missing and `unexplained` 0 / 0, at 400 files and at full corpus. The general form, for the next rule of this shape: **where two transformations must both apply, the order is part of the specification** — and an exhaustive sweep that ignores that will trade one defect for another.

decisions.wave: 16 - the LAST unexplained edge in 3,839 files, and it was the analyzer's
decisions.status: FIXED on BOTH sides - a builtin-looking name the file DECLARES is a user type
decisions.observation: After Z56 the full corpus held exactly one unexplained edge: `references (declared-type) -> u8` at `zig/test/behavior/basic.zig:635`.
decisions.analysis: The source is three lines: `const @"u8" = u16; const c: @"u8" = 300;` — a user-declared file-scope type alias whose name is a builtin. The analyzer published the reference (correct) and the TRUTH dropped it, because its builtin exclusion is purely name-based and cannot see that the file declares the name. Fixing the truth alone then produced one MISSING (`references -> f80` in zls/Interner.zig), which located the same blindness on the OTHER side — and the real shape: the ANALYZER's filter was decided by SPELLING. `@"u8"` (quoted) slipped past the name filter while plain `f80` did not, so whether a user's own type reached the declared-type graph depended on whether they had quoted it.
decisions.resolution: Both sides now ask the same question in the same way: is this name declared at FILE SCOPE in this file? The analyzer gained `zigFileScopeNames(root)` — tree-derived, memoised per root, function-locals excluded — and the truth mirrors it. The set had to be FILE-SCOPE on both sides: the first truth version collected function-LOCALS too, so one `var u8` inside any function let every genuine builtin `u8` reference through and MISSING went 0 -> 1.
decisions.cost: Third instance this session of a name-keyed rule that cannot see local declarations — after #963 and the quoting family — and the seventh time in this lane that a 'declared names' set needed a scope rule attached to it. Fixing one side of a comparison and not the other did not produce a wrong number; it produced the OTHER number, which is the clearest possible statement of why both sides must be fixed together. And the F1 grammar audit caught me reintroducing the dead `field_identifier` disjunct that Z45 had removed, in the very gate that exists to report such leftovers — which is the fifth time in this lane that a gate earned its place by failing on something I had just written.

decisions.wave: 16 - a shared register that said this lane still had a regex it retired in Z18
decisions.status: FIXED - the ghost row is retired, with its reason recorded rather than deleted silently
decisions.observation: `script/m49/verify-r2-regex.ts` reports `register has no ghost rows -- 3 ghost, first: real-zig-analyzer.ts | /[!*\s\[\]\{\}]+/g (1/0)`. The Zig analyzer has had **zero** regex operations since Z18, verified by direct scan — and the M49 debt register still carried a row for `real-zig-analyzer.ts:1016` claiming otherwise, re-anchored across four waves (systems wave 5c71e176, M49.R2 freshness 840ffbbb, M59.A7 line round e7697acd, a 2026-09-26 merge).
decisions.analysis: A register row is a CLAIM, and a claim that is never retired becomes a permanent fact about a lane that stopped being true weeks earlier. Four separate waves re-anchored its LINE NUMBER, each preserving the claim — so the row's own history is a record of the cost of not retiring it.
